label: Reserved gold maximum
summary: Compares the size that the character's 'reserved' gold budget is supposed to reach.
details: Compare it with <, <=, =, !=, > or >=. The game's description is badly worded, so this reading rests on the game's documentation and the key name; what the 'reserved' budget is used for is not explained.

label: Has reserved treasury
summary: Whether the character has the treasury that the 'reserved' category requires.
details: Works on a character. The game's documentation names the AI category 'reserved' and allows the comparison operators <, <=, =, !=, > and >=, but it does not say what is compared or what the required amount is. Vanilla does not use it.

label: Reserved treasury maximum
summary: Compares the size that the character's 'reserved' treasury budget is supposed to reach.
details: Compare it with <, <=, =, !=, > or >=. The game's description is badly worded, so this reading rests on the game's documentation and the key name; what the 'reserved' budget is used for is not explained.

label: Has reserved treasury or gold
summary: Whether the character has the treasury that the 'reserved' category requires, or their gold if they do not use a treasury.
details: The game's documentation contrasts it with the plain treasury check only by the gold fallback for characters without a treasury. It allows the comparison operators <, <=, =, !=, > and >=, but does not say what the required amount is. Vanilla does not use it.

label: Target has opinion modifier of character
summary: Whether the target character has the given opinion modifier on the character being checked.
details: The target is the one who holds the opinion, and the checked character is the one it is about. The game's documentation also allows comparing the modifier's value (`value >= X`) or giving a range (`value = { MIN MAX }`, both ends included). Vanilla uses it with modifiers such as an ignored eviction or an exposed unfaithful spouse.

fields.name: modifier
fields.text: The opinion modifier to look for.

fields.name: target
fields.text: The character who holds the opinion.
fields.values: a character, such as root or scope:target

fields.name: value
fields.text: Optional check on the modifier's value.
fields.values: a comparison like `>= 10`, or a range `{ MIN MAX }`

label: Their opinion of the character
summary: Compares how much the target character likes the character being checked.
details: The target's opinion of the checked character is read, not the other way round. Opinion can be negative. The game's documentation allows a comparison (`value >= 20`) or a range (`value = { min max }`). Vanilla most often checks `>= 0` or `< 0`.

fields.name: target
fields.text: The character whose opinion is read.
fields.values: a character, such as root or scope:target

fields.name: value
fields.values: a comparison like `>= 50`, or a range `{ min max }`

label: Can pick a doctrine
summary: Whether the rite is allowed to pick the given doctrine.
details: It checks both whether the doctrine is shown and whether it can be picked, using the head of the rite as the reference character. Works on a rite.

label: Can pick a tenet
summary: Whether the rite is allowed to pick the given tenet as a core tenet.
details: It checks both whether the tenet is shown and whether it can be picked, using the head of the rite as the reference character. Works on a rite. Vanilla gives the tenet through a saved scope.

label: Rite's counties
summary: Compares how many counties the rite controls.
details: Compare it with <, <=, =, !=, > or >=. Vanilla mostly checks `>= 1`, meaning the rite controls at least one county.

label: Rite fulfillment score
summary: Compares the character's spiritual fulfillment score for the given rite.
details: The score is read for the checked character and the target rite. Vanilla compares it against steps like 0, 25, 50 and 75. The game's documentation shows two forms, a block with `target` and `value`, and a function-like form `rite_fulfillment_score(scope:some_rite) > 50`.

fields.name: target
fields.text: The rite the score is for.

label: Of a gender allowed as clergy
summary: Whether the target character is of a gender that is allowed to be clergy of the rite.
details: Works on a rite; the character is given as the value. Vanilla usually passes `prev` or `root`.

label: Has culture
summary: Whether the rite is associated with the given culture.
details: Works on a rite; the culture is given as the value. The game documents no more than this, and vanilla gives no examples here.

label: Has doctrine
summary: Whether the rite has the given doctrine.
details: Works on a rite; write the doctrine key as the value. It is one of the most used checks in vanilla, for example for pluralism, gender dominance or theocracy doctrines.

label: Of the ruling gender
summary: Whether the target character's gender is a dominant ruling gender of the rite.
details: It is also true when the rite has no dominant ruling gender at all. Works on a rite; the character is given as the value, mostly `prev` in vanilla.

label: Has doctrine parameter
summary: Whether the rite has the given parameter, set by any of its core tenets or doctrines.
details: Both core tenets and doctrines are searched. Write the parameter key as the value. Vanilla uses it a lot, for example for `witchcraft_accepted` or `clergy_must_be_female`.

label: Of the preferred clergy gender
summary: Whether the target character is of the gender the rite prefers for its clergy.
details: Works on a rite; the character is given as the value. Vanilla has no uses of it, so this rests on the game's documentation alone.

label: Has tenet
summary: Whether the rite has the given tenet as one of its core tenets.
details: Works on a rite; write the tenet key as the value. Only core tenets count. The documented example names it `has_tenet`, which looks like a slip.

label: Hostility to another rite
summary: Compares how hostile the rite is towards another rite.
details: Vanilla compares the level with the named levels `faith_astray_level`, `faith_hostile_level` and `faith_evil_level`, usually with `>=`. The other rite is often written like `scope:actor.rite`.

fields.name: target
fields.text: The rite the hostility is measured towards.

fields.name: value
fields.text: The hostility level to compare with.

label: Compare hostility to two rites
summary: Compares the rite's hostility towards two other rites.
details: The game's documentation shows only the form `rite_hostility_level_comparison { rite1 > rite2 }`; presumably it asks whether the hostility towards the first is higher than towards the second, but the game's documentation does not say. Vanilla has no uses, so the exact fields are not confirmed.

label: Rite's religion
summary: Whether the rite belongs to the given religion.
details: Write the religion key as the value, such as `christianity_religion` or `islam_religion`. Works on a rite.

label: Same secret type as
summary: Whether the secret being checked is of the same type as another secret.
details: Works on a secret; give the other secret as the value, for example `scope:some_secret`.

label: Save opinion as a name
summary: Saves how much the checked character likes a target character, under a name you choose, to be referenced later in the same trigger.
details: Vanilla uses it with targets such as a diarch successor or an actor's top liege, and names like `actor_opinion_temp` or `vassal_opinion`. The game's documentation text is cut off, so the fields come from vanilla's use.

fields.name: name
fields.text: The name to save the opinion under.

fields.name: target
fields.text: The character whose opinion of the checked character is read.
fields.values: a character, such as root or scope:actor.top_liege

label: Save as a temporary scope
summary: Saves the current thing under a name, so later parts of the same trigger can refer to it as `scope:name`.
details: The saved name only lasts while the trigger runs. It is one of the most used keys in vanilla, with names like `char_temp` and `county_check`.

label: Save a temporary value
summary: Saves a number or a yes/no value under a name you choose, for use later in the same trigger.
details: The documented wording mentions an effect, but this is the trigger version of the key. Vanilla saves numbers, script values and `flag:` values this way.

fields.name: name
fields.text: The name to save the value under.

fields.name: value
fields.values: a number, a yes/no, or a script value

label: Scheme agent charges
summary: Compares how many agent charges the scheme currently has available.
details: Compare it with <, <=, =, !=, > or >=. Vanilla mostly checks it against a cap value, or `>= 1`. One vanilla use is a block with `value` and `subtract`; the game's documentation does not cover that form, so what `subtract` does exactly is not stated.

label: Scheme breaches
summary: Compares how many breaches the scheme currently has.
details: Compare it with <, <=, =, !=, > or >=. Vanilla only uses it twice, against a limit value.

label: Scheme age in days
summary: Compares how many days have passed since the scheme started.
details: Compare it with <, <=, =, !=, > or >=. Vanilla mostly checks it against a minimum time before agent events can happen.

label: Is agent of the scheme
summary: Whether the target character is part of this scheme.
details: Works on a scheme; the character is given as the value, mostly `prev` in vanilla.

label: Exposed agents
summary: Compares how many of the scheme's agents are exposed.
details: Compare it with <, <=, =, !=, > or >=. Vanilla does not use it, so what 'exposed' means is only as the game's documentation says.

label: Agents in the scheme
summary: Compares how many agents the scheme has.
details: Compare it with <, <=, =, !=, > or >=. Vanilla checks for at least one or two agents.

label: Scheme phase duration
summary: Compares the length of the scheme's phase.
details: Compare it with <, <=, =, !=, > or >=. The game gives no unit. Vanilla does not use it as a key of its own, but it appears as a value (`scope:scheme.scheme_phase_duration`) in comparisons of `scheme_progress`.

label: Scheme progress
summary: Compares how far along the scheme is, on a scale from 0 to 10.
details: Compare it with <, <=, =, !=, > or >=. Vanilla compares it with named steps such as `scheme_progress_33`, `scheme_progress_50` and `scheme_progress_66`, and sometimes with the scheme's phase duration.

label: Scheme secrecy
summary: Compares the secrecy of the scheme.
details: Compare it with <, <=, =, !=, > or >=. Vanilla does not use it and the game gives no range.

label: Scheme skill
summary: Checks the scheme against a skill name; vanilla writes skills such as `intrigue` or `martial` here.
details: The game's documentation describes something else (a scheme modifier, with `has_scheme_modifier = X`), which does not match how vanilla uses the key. Going by the values vanilla writes, it most likely asks whether the scheme uses that skill, but the game does not say so.

label: Scheme success chance
summary: Compares the scheme's success chance.
details: Compare it with <, <=, =, !=, > or >=. Vanilla uses it once, against the maximum scheme success chance.

label: Scheme type
summary: Whether the scheme is of the given type.
details: Write the scheme type key as the value, such as `murder`, `abduct`, `seduce` or `befriend`. Works on a scheme.

label: Running scripted tests
summary: Whether the game is currently running its scripted tests.
details: Takes `yes` or `no`. It is meant for the game's own testing.

label: Can marry (test)
summary: Whether the character can marry the target character.
details: The name marks it as a helper for the game's scripted tests. Works on a character; the other character is given as the value. Vanilla does not use it.

label: Base dread (test)
summary: Compares the character's baseline dread value.
details: The name marks it as a helper for the game's scripted tests. Compare it with <, <=, =, !=, > or >=. Vanilla does not use it.

label: Tax income without theocracy (test)
summary: Compares the character's tax income, leaving out income from the theocratic lessee.
details: The name marks it as a helper for the game's scripted tests. Compare it with <, <=, =, !=, > or >=. Vanilla does not use it.
